The Emancipation Proclamation. An executive order issued by President Abraham Lincoln on January first, 1863, during the American Civil War, declaring all slaves in Confederate states forever free. The order applied only to slaves in the rebelling Southern states, not to slaves in the Union-loyal border states or those under Union occupation. While the proclamation did not immediately free all enslaved people—enforcement depended on Union military victory—it transformed the Civil War from a war for the Union into a war for emancipation and paved the way for the Thirteenth Amendment, which abolished slavery nationwide.

Lincoln first issued the Preliminary Emancipation Proclamation on September twenty-second, 1862, after the Union's victory at the Battle of Antietam. He gave the Confederacy one hundred days to rejoin the Union or lose their enslaved workers. The final Emancipation Proclamation came on January first, 1863, declaring all slaves in Confederate states are and henceforward shall be free. It applied to the ten Confederate states—South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, Texas, Virginia, Arkansas, and North Carolina—but not to slavery in Union-loyal border states like Maryland, Delaware, Kentucky, and Missouri.

Lincoln justified the proclamation as a military necessity, a war measure intended to weaken the Confederate economy and bolster Union military strength. The proclamation encouraged enslaved people to escape to Union lines and authorized the recruitment of formerly enslaved people into the Union Army, known as the United States Colored Troops. Approximately one hundred eighty thousand African American soldiers served in the Union Army and Navy during the war, many of them formerly enslaved.

The proclamation did not legally free all enslaved people—it was a war measure that would be superseded by the Thirteenth Amendment, ratified in 1865.
